p: Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie was born on 25 June 1936 in Parepare, South Sulawesi, the son of Alwi Abdul Jalil Habibie, an agriculturist of Bugis-Gorontalese descent, and R. A. Tuti Marini Puspowardojo, a Javanese noblewoman from Yogyakarta. He began to study aviation at Delft in the Netherlands but, because of the dispute between the two countries over West New Guinea, moved to the Technische Hochschule Aachen in Germany, where he took an engineer's degree in 1960 and a doctorate in aerospace engineering in 1965. In 1962 he married Hasri Ainun Besari, a medical doctor.

He joined Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm in Hamburg, where he worked on the Airbus A-300B and reached a middle management post in 1974. That year President Suharto recruited him to return as part of a drive to industrialise Indonesia. Two years later he became head of the new state aircraft maker, known as IPTN, which built Puma helicopters and CASA planes and in 1995 produced a small passenger aircraft, the N-250, a commercial failure.

From 1978 he was state minister of research and technology. By 1991 he oversaw ten state-owned industries, among them shipbuilding, steel, arms and energy; an estimate of 1993 put their cost at nearly 2 billion dollars a year in state funds. In 1990 he was elected the first chair of the Indonesian Association of Muslim Intellectuals, a modernist organisation that gave him a political base. When Suharto signalled in January 1998, during the Asian financial crisis, that he wanted him as vice-president, the rupiah fell.

As president he also forbade the official use of the terms pribumi and non-pribumi, lifted restrictions on the teaching of Mandarin Chinese and passed laws giving autonomy to regencies and cities. He had opposed independence for East Timor and offered special autonomy; the armed forces' leaders were not consulted on his decision to hold a referendum. After the vote of 30 August 1999 pro-Indonesian militias killed and displaced large numbers of people, and on 12 September he accepted a peacekeeping force mandated by the United Nations.

A leaked telephone call with his attorney general raised doubts about the investigation of Suharto. The Bank Bali scandal of 1999, in which bank funds reached members of his re-election team, damaged him further. In October 1999 the assembly known as the MPR rejected his accountability speech by 355 votes to 322, and he withdrew his candidacy; Abdurrahman Wahid succeeded him. He died in the Gatot Soebroto Army Hospital on 11 September 2019 and was buried at the Kalibata Heroes' Cemetery beside his wife.

notes: The article gives only the abbreviation MPR and never expands it, and names the hospital without its city; the text keeps to that.

The third section covers the presidency's remaining acts, the fall and the death under 'Death and legacy'; 'Career' could be split differently, but the description already tells the main acts of the presidency.
The article says the reform laws 'set elections for December 1999' while the lead says an early election was held; I left the election date out.
General Wiranto's alleged coup threat of 10 September is left out (the article says 'allegedly').
